#8427. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

“The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”

Actually, big is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

“I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a big challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

“I just set it and left it,” she said. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

“As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she said. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she said of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”

As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she said.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.)

And in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case said. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”

#8426. A Hiker Fell off a Cliff in Big Bend National Park. Then Rescuers Had to Leave Him There Overnight.

Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard)

A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Big Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.

According to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders. Rescuers reached the area just after 9 P.M. and called the Georgia Army National Guard medical evacuation crew assigned to the Joint Task Force-Southern Border. The organization works with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor the shared border between Texas and Mexico, an area central to a heated national debate over the Trump Administration’s border wall construction.

The helicopter crew had taken off, but with limited lighting and winds approaching 35 miles per hour, and a string of storms moving into the area, the Black Hawk medevac crew made the difficult decision to scrub the mission.

“The crew agreed it was not safe and we had to make the unfortunate decision to go back and try again in the daylight,” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gregory Hiett, the aircraft commander, said in a statement. “It was an extremely difficult thing to do, knowing the patient was going to be stuck out there for the rest of the night.”

Throughout the night, park responders remained on-scene and on the ground.

Just after 9 A.M. on November 14, a second helicopter mission launched with a hoist rescue team. Flight medic and technician Holly Johnson descended 150 feet on a cable, determined the hiker was uninjured, and secured him in a rescue vest to lift him into the aircraft. The mission was finished by 10:45 A.M., and the hiker was transferred to Big Bend Regional Medical Center.

“During a complex hoist operation in rugged, inaccessible terrain, our medevac crew successfully reached and evacuated an injured hiker when no ground rescue option existed, delivering the patient safely to higher medical care,” Lt. Col. Teresa Parrotta, commander of the 29th Combat Aviation Brigade, Maryland Army National Guard, said in a statement.

Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city. It’s rugged, isolated, and enormous, spanning 800,000 acres with sheer 1,500-foot limestone cliffs. The National Park Service warns visitors to expect unreliable cell service, sparse infrastructure, and primitive roads—conditions compounded by the intense Chihuahuan Desert sandwiched between the Chisos Mountains. Reaching a hiking trailhead is challenging because roads frequently wash out from flash flooding, and many backcountry trails require high-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles.

#8425. How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

When I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

But as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more important. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin says.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

Perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

Scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s important to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

Before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

Loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin says. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

“When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney says. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

When descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

With your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

Keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

You might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”

“It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin says. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”

It comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

Rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

And before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

“The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney says. “You can just sort of ride it.”

On a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

When surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

On particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

“I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin says. “I never feel like I have that much control.”

Martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

If you’re shouldering a particularly big pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

But if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.

#8424. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun)

There is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

This is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a big-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

I watched The Alpinist on the big screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

#8423. UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

The 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

There are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

For the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:

Race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

Two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI announced the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”

The discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its new mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

The 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

This will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

From the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti says. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”

But coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti says. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he says.

Overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB.  “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”

American Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”

If there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne said.

For spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”

Could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this new schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour company Run the Alps.

#8421. 5 Gifts for the Practical Person on Your List

An easy way to identify the best gifts? The ones that are still in use long after the decorations come down. That’s the appeal of a good tool. Not because it’s flashy, but because it becomes part of someone’s everyday routine.

That’s what makes a Leatherman such an easy gift to give. With options ranging from minimalist everyday-carry knives to fully featured multitools, there’s a model for every personality on your list.

Better yet, select Leatherman favorites are 20 percent off through December 31, exclusively at Leatherman.com. During the brand’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday promotion (November 19-30), shoppers can also receive a free lanyard bead with orders over $125 or a free Bit Kit with orders over $225.

For the person who values versatility but travels light, the Skeletool CX is an everyday-carry upgrade they’ll actually use. Think travelers, hikers, cyclists, and anyone who likes being prepared without dedicating half a pocket to a tool. The Skeletool KBX takes the simplicity of the KB and adds a little grit. Its combo blade pairs a straight edge with a serrated section, making it a natural fit for people who put their gear to work. Whether they’re restoring an old piece of furniture, tying custom flies, or bringing a long-neglected project across the finish line, the Rebar is ready to help. Give the Rebar to the person who would rather figure it out themselves than wait for someone else to do it.

Some people have a reputation for being prepared. Get that person on your list the Wave Plus. What sets it apart is accessibility: many of its most-used tools can be opened with one hand and accessed without unfolding the entire tool, making quick adjustments and repairs that much easier. #8420. Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman)

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

“All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he says. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

“The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he launched his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

“The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.)

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he said, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

“Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”

Zartman says he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design new testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”

#8418. What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan)

On the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected. The terrain was brutal, with steep descents over sharp, rocky granite tracks along the 6,345-foot Jebel Jais summit. My heavy pack weighed me down, and I could feel every stone beneath my boots. By day three, my two big toes hurt so much that on one challenging descent, I collapsed and couldn’t take another step.

That’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me. He saw that I was struggling and stopped to pull out a roll of tape from his bag. Then, he peeled off my very stinky hiking socks without a second thought, taped up my toes, and bandaged my knees. He even carried my pack for several miles, guiding me down the remaining steep sections.

This stranger had no reason to go out of his way to help me, and I know I could not have finished that day without him. Hikers call this kind of experience “trail magic.” The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines the term as any instance of finding what you need most when you least expect it; experiencing something rare, extraordinary, or inspiring in nature, or encountering unexpected acts of generosity that restore one’s faith in humanity.

Trail magic is often associated with Appalachian Trail history from the early 1980s. However, after my experience in the UAE, I started wondering what it looks like elsewhere. So, here are five stories from other hikers who have experienced trail magic in one form or another around the world.

Matt Jordan, a hiking and backpacking guide with Intrepid Travel, was walking New Zealand’s 1,881-mile Te Araroa Trail southbound in 2023 when he hit the muddy Longwood Forest in Fiordland. After a miserable day of rain and bog, he pushed on toward Turnbull’s Hut, one of the last backcountry huts on that segment. He’d heard that sometimes, free supplies were stored there for hikers passing through. As he approached, he prayed it hadn’t already all been taken by the time he got there.

“Thankfully it hadn’t,” he says. When he opened the store area, he found a cache of goodies.

“A local man who hikes in supplies, hauls out trash, and maintains the hut about twice a month leaves coolers stocked with beer, soda, and candy bars,” Jordan says. Excitedly, he grabbed a drink, then promptly slipped in the mud and fell on his backside. After days of awful weather conditions, though, that didn’t stop him from laughing out loud.

“For me, the gesture was about more than a cold drink. It was a reminder of the generosity of strangers and the sense of community that makes long-distance hikes unforgettable worldwide.”

Meeta Singh Rao, a hiking guide in India, says some of her best trail magic came from shepherds who spend months in the high mountain pastures of the Indian Himalayas. In October 2022, she was leading a trek to Nawali Bugyal in Uttarakhand when the weather turned. Heavy rain began to fall, and strong winds blew. The mules carrying their gear were also lost, and camp was miles away.

The group came across a shepherd with his flock. He heard where they were headed, and offered them shelter in his channi, a mountain hut made of stone, mud, and plastic sheets. “When rainwater leaked through the roof, he walked out into the downpour to rearrange the plastic so we stayed dry,” says Rao.

When Rao offered to pay, the shepherd gently refused, saying they were his guests. “A couple with so little of their own opened their home to us, giving us a feeling of belonging in the mountains,” she adds.

Kaitlyn Bussell has walked four Caminos. But her second, the 62-mile Camino Inglés in September 2023 through Galicia, was particularly challenging. The rain was constant, few hostels and cafés were open in the fall, and she walked long stretches without seeing another pilgrim.

On the second day, wet and ready for a break, she ducked into the first bar she found for a café con leche and to charge her phone. When she went to pay, the young woman behind the counter told her the coffee was free and handed her some water, prayer cards and a small Camino keepsake.

“It was a small thing, but it came at exactly the right moment,” Bussell recalls. “After days of rain, it lifted my spirits and made me realize that this pilgrimage is as much about the people you meet as it is the miles you walk.”

On Japan’s Shikoku 88 Temples Pilgrimage route, Lauren Roerick and her brother were leaving one of the temples when she spotted a sign offering matcha tea ceremonies for pilgrims. They initially walked away unsure whether they would be intruding but returned and decided to try it anyway.

“A Japanese man welcomed us inside where two women in kimonos were preparing and serving matcha under his instruction,” adds Roerick. “To make us feel welcome, he called a friend and had her on speakerphone, translating the whole ceremony from Japanese into English.” Lauren and her brother learned about the tradition, tried making tea themselves, and ate small Japanese sweets.

“It was proof that trail magic isn’t always a bottle of water or a helping hand,” says Roerick. “Sometimes a stranger opens his door, works around a language barrier, and shares a bit of culture with people passing through.”

On a windy hike to Matterhorn Base Camp, Libera Pagano, tour director with EF Adventures, noticed an older woman struggling. The altitude made her dizzy, her legs were shaking, and her friend had walked far ahead. “I offered to sit with the woman while she rested behind a large rock and we started chatting,” says Pagano.

That’s when Pagano learned it was the woman’s 86th birthday, and the hike was a present she’d given herself. They stayed together, and when the woman felt ready, they walked slowly until they caught up with her companion. When the group met back at basecamp, the woman told Pagano that without her help, she would never have made it to the summit.

“I thought nothing of what I had done,” says Pagano. “But for that woman, it was the difference between giving up and fulfilling her birthday wish.”

I never learned the name of the man who bandaged my toes in the Hajar Mountains, and I probably never will. But I think about him whenever I struggle on a trail or see another hiker limping.

All these stories have one thing in common—human compassion. Sometimes that is stopping to help a stranger in need, sharing what little you have, or leaving a cache of supplies for a hiker you’ll probably never meet. These gestures don’t have to be grand or cost much, but they can make an enormous difference and are an easy thing to pay forward so everyone experiences a little magic outdoors.

#8417. How Does La Sportiva’s Newest Approach Shoe Stack Up? I Took It to the High Sierra and French Alps to Find Out.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-new TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

The breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

#8416. Cut Off for 6 Years, Denali’s Only Road and Its Wildest Country Are Reopen for 2027

The single road in Denali National Park winds through the heart of the park and ends in the remote historic mining town of Kantishna. Hikers and cyclists are now able to cross the newly completed Pretty Rocks Bridge, and full public park bus service is set to resume in 2027. (Photo: Pursuit)

“Bear! On the left!” I jolt forward from the front passenger seat to find where our driver has spotted a grizzly on the open tundra. On a steep slope covered with birch trees, pops of autumn amber and rust scattered against green spruce trees, I can make out a moving boulder—then I spot its golden blonde fur. Olivia Juarez, general manager of Denali Backcountry Lodge, tells me it’s the signature coat of Denali grizzlies. Juarez is driving three of us, including her dog, on the entire 92-mile nearly unpaved stretch of the Denali Park Road, which feels precarious at times due to two-thirds of it being only one lane. But the speed limit is 35 mph, and we are the only ones on it.

For the last six years, this mostly gravel mountain corridor—the only road through Denali National Park and Preserve—has been closed after mile 43 due to a landslide. But in time for the 2027 summer season, access to the full 92 miles will reopen, allowing visitors to explore the depths of Denali’s backcountry once again.

Juarez slows the van to a stop, and we pass around binoculars. The grizzly is far in the distance, but it’s what surrounds it in every direction that catches my breath: striking volcanic cliffs in a kaleidoscope of earthy hues and gravelly, braided glacial streams stretching across an endless expanse of wild. It’s only us on the road, and this grizzly out yonder, for as far as we can see. And out there, somewhere hidden under a cloak of clouds, is Denali, or The Great One, as the peak’s traditional name translates from the Koyukon Athabascan language.

On September 2, 2026, the long-awaited Pretty Rocks Bridge in Denali National Park was completed, an architectural marvel that bypasses the still-active landslide. At 475 feet long and 24 feet wide, the steel single-span truss bridge is just wide enough for a park bus to drive through.

This $230 million federal project includes 23 underground thermosiphons—a passive cooling technology that pulls heat out of the earth to keep the permafrost frozen year-round. Pedestrians and cyclists are currently permitted to cross, with full bus and vehicle service scheduled to resume in 2027.

I’ve spent the last four nights at Denali Backcountry Lodge, a remote all-inclusive outpost that sits at the end of the road. I flew in via a 45-mile helicopter ride, the only way guests can reach the property since the landslide. The lodge is the farthest place you can stay and still be in the park. We spent our days hiking through the spongy tundra, exploring the history of the Kantishna mining camp, and kayaking Wonder Lake with Denali in the background, a coveted sight since it was photographed by Ansel Adams on a rare cloudless day in 1947.

Since the road closure, no one other than guests staying at the three remote wilderness lodges has been able to visit these iconic areas of the park. While Denali Backcountry Lodge offers a chance to truly settle into the wild, all the excitement is found along the road. That is, nearly all our wildlife sightings (except for a grizzly sitting atop its moose kill spotted in the distance on one of our guided hikes) happened on a drive: a trio of caribou running, a moose moving through the willow marshes, a porcupine waddling across the road, a bear cub prancing out from the shrubs.

Starting in 2027, visitors will finally be able to reach the end of the road again on a Denali park bus. Guests staying at Denali Backcountry Lodge will arrive and depart via a private bus next year, and their Creekside Cabins guests will take a private bus in and fly out on a single-engine bush plane. Day guests will be able to reach the end of the road and book a guided experience at Denali Backcountry Lodge.

More travelers returning to Denali’s backcountry means there’s more opportunity to transform them into stewards of this land. “Visiting a place like this is life-changing for people,” says Alexa Donahe, vice president and general manager of Pursuit’s Alaska Collection, which includes Denali Backcountry Lodge. “Day traffic allows for more people who don’t have the time or resources to have an immersive backcountry experience like this and to experience the depths of the wilderness for a day.”

Even with more visitors coming in by bus, it will still feel remote, says Donahe. There will be strict park (and lodge) restrictions to preserve the landscape and wildlife. For comparison, more than 4 million people visit 2.2-million-acre Yellowstone yearly, with easy road access for private cars. Only 500,000 people visit Denali each year, but at 6 million acres, the park is the size of Vermont.

Sure, there are more people gathering at the park entrance, where you’ll find a visitor center and the famous Denali sled dogs, but once you reach the dirt road, it feels as remote as ever.

Only about 30 percent of visitors to Denali National Park and Preserve get a completely clear view of the peak. An even smaller subset—fewer than ten percent—experience a completely cloud-free, base-to-summit view. Visitors who stay multiple days (such as four days in Kantishna) see the mountain at much higher rates, around 85 percent. Because the massive 20,310-foot peak creates its own local weather system, heavy cloud cover frequently obscures the summit, especially during the summer tourism season.

One morning at breakfast, a group of Natural Habitat guests wait out bad weather to depart. Their expedition leader Samantha Strauss shares with me her thoughts on the fully opened Denali. “For every person who comes out and sees this place, that’s one more person that cares about public lands. Especially right now, public lands are not promised to us,” she says. “Even if that means I have less square mileage allotted just to myself, even if that means I have to share this space with more people, it is a conservation win because it helps people create a connection to the landscape and have a stake in its future.”

I flew over Denali National Park in a helicopter and left on the Denali Park Road, just days after the Pretty Rocks Bridge bypassing the landslide was completed. Both ways gave me different perspectives on this vast expanse of raw wilderness.

While it was thrilling to soar over glaciers and peaks, it was seeing Denali from the ground, my eyes scanning the landscape for wildlife, moving through the changing early autumn hues, feeling the rush of brisk air as I rolled my window down to take a photo, that made me feel I was a part of it. The road is the center line of this wilderness, and it’s not only the best way to see Denali’s untamed backcountry and wildlife, but to feel its beating heart.

#8414. Make Uphills Easier With These Exercises for Explosive Strength

Hills don’t just feel hard. Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground. If you’ve got that one hiking buddy who seems to power up the hills while you’re huffing and puffing, the reason isn’t just that they’re fit. It’s that they’ve built up power—specifically explosive strength, which is fitness jargon for their ability to quickly muster the strength they’ve built. Explosive strength is the same stuff you use when you jump, bound, or push yourself up a steep step.

“On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” says Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete. “If you don’t have the ability to hit those little power spikes over and over and over again, that’s a much greater determinant of uphill performance.”

Explosive strength can be trained, though. In a small 2011 study of women in their 60s and 70s published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity, one group was assigned to lift weights in a way that would build explosive strength. After 12 weeks, those women climbed stairs 17 percent faster than they did at the beginning of the study.

“Uphills are hard, and they’re hard for everyone,” says Mike Aidala, coach and owner of The Offense, a gym and mindset coaching business in Boulder, CO. He says that approaching your training with a goal of getting stronger, rather than faster, can help build uphill power.

Here’s a mental intent method from the study that can make every exercise build more explosive strength, and six specific exercises for building explosive, uphill strength from Viada, Aidala, and Rose Wetzel, a certified personal trainer and pro Spartan racer with multiple world championship podium finishes.

Explosive exercises are usually those where your body leaves the floor (like squat jumps or box jumps) or a weight leaves your hands (like medicine ball throws). But you can achieve the same benefit by performing the concentric phase—the “lift” phase—of any exercise with explosive intent. That’s how the elderly participants in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity study built power. On each repetition of machine exercises, they did the eccentric—or “lowering”—portion of the lift at a controlled pace, and then they pushed the weight up in an explosive manner.

Lifting weights in this way gives a two-way boost to your uphill performance. Not only does it build power in the “push” portion of each lift, but lowering weights slowly and under control increases the strength of your tendons.

“When we train our tendons, we’re able to be more explosive,” says Wetzel. Stronger tendons, she says, “help with the body’s ability to spring off the ground, to explode off with all that strength.”

You can use this method with almost every strength exercise you do, says Viada. His recommendation: Start with a few sets of each exercise with explosive intent, and then move into your “regular” sets of the move. During the explosive sets, he says, don’t use as much weight as you will in the later, “normal” sets.

For a starting weight, Viada suggests subtracting 25 percent from the maximum weight with which you could normally perform 10 reps. For example, if you regularly do 10 leg presses with 200 pounds, perform your explosive reps with 150 pounds.

In addition to using a lower weight, Viada also recommends doing fewer repetitions in each set. While you could probably do this weight for 15 or more repetitions, start with a handful, and make sure each one is done with maximum explosive intention.

“The only thing that matters is that they’re explosive and they’re fast,” he says. “So when you go to the bottom of the movement, think about suddenly trying to push the bar or sled up through a wall. Pretend you’re trying to smash [the weight] up through the ceiling.”

Do a few sets in this way for each move, then move to your normal, longer sets with your regular weights.

Our experts recommend these six moves to become more explosive and more stable as you trek or run uphill—they’re moves the coaches have used to train clients to climb 14ers, and that Wetzel herself has used to vault her way to multiple obstacle course race podiums.

The first four exercises can be done anywhere, including as part of a run or hike warmup. For the last two, you’ll need some gym equipment.

These jumps let you practice exploding, but also train your knee not to wobble on each step. Not only will a stable knee help prevent injuries when you’re thrown off-kilter on the trail, but will prevent you from losing energy that could be used to propel you forward.

Do one set of 10 jumps per leg three to four times per week. Over time, try to minimize wobbling, and then increase the distance of your jumps.

Similar to the previous exercise, these jumps incorporate side-to-side movement. Don’t rush through them, Aidala says. Land, get stable, take a beat, then repeat.

Do 10 jumps in each direction on each leg. Perform these three to four times per week.

These aren’t the plodding high knees you’re used to, Wetzel says.

“When I do these drills, it’s for a very short amount of time, and I do them for power,” she says. “I’m not doing high knees like someone might do for 30 seconds to get their heart rate up … it’s like six to eight seconds of hot potato, hot potato, hot potato, and then catch my breath for 30 seconds.”

You can do these before every run or hike, or as a warmup before any workout.

This move, Wetzel says, helps you to feel like you can spring off with each step up a hill. Unlike a longer jumping lunge, she does these mini lunges as quickly as possible, keeping the movement “fierce, short, and explosive.” Instead of dropping into a full lunge, bend your knees only slightly, with your feet moving front to back almost like you’re cross-country skiing while jumping slightly.

Do a few sets of 16 reps before every run, hike, or gym workout.

“Uphill running starts from the hips,” Viada says. “And with Bulgarian split squat hops, when you start that explosiveness from the bottom, you’ll explosively engage those hips like nothing else.”

This takes one of the most dreaded moves in the gym and adds an explosive element, with the front foot leaving the ground on each repetition. Your foot doesn’t need to come way off the ground, though, Viada says. An inch or so is great. Since it’s already a tough move, he recommends using a light weight, or no weight at all.

Perform three to four sets of four to five hops per leg, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these two to three times per week.

When lifting with explosive intent, coaches often recommend that you “explode out of the hole,” or the bottom of the move. With the Anderson squat, you start in the hole using a squat rack, pressing the bar off pins so you can focus even more on the powerful concentric portion of the lift.

Don’t set the stops on the rack too low, Viada says. Aim so that when you get under the bar, your knees are bent 90 degrees, mimicking the angles you’ll need to hike uphill with power.

Perform three to four sets of four to five squats, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these one to two times per week.

#8412. Gary Colliver Was a “Big-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions)

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

To Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”

Colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management plan for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

“There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial plan was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

As a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular big wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

#8407. A Basset Hound Showed Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation)

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in New York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

The day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

New York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

But time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with plans to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

When the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

Finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

“This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”

Foutch said that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

“It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch said. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”

The hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

People with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, said there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

“In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly says. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”

Wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he says SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody quickly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”

He says e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

Urgency is particularly important in these cases, Cooper says. Research shows that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

That’s why Cooper says, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.
